desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

The score of a list is the sum of |x - y| over every pair of neighbouring nodes x, y (a list with fewer than two nodes has score 0).

You may reverse at most one contiguous range of nodes (possibly empty or a single node, which changes nothing). Return the largest score you can obtain.

For [2,3,1,5,4] the score is 1+2+4+1 = 8. Reversing the range at positions 2 to 4 (1-indexed) gives [2,5,1,3,4] with score 3+4+2+1 = 10, which is the best, so the answer is 10. Checking every range with a full recount is O(n3); a linear solution exists.
hints: Reversing a range keeps all differences inside the range (only their order changes). Only the two boundary pairs change.

Reversing positions l..r replaces the boundary differences |a[l-1]-a[l]| + |a[r]-a[r+1]| by |a[l-1]-a[r]| + |a[l]-a[r+1]|. Handle the cases l = 1 and r = n (only one boundary) separately. That already gives an O(n<sup>2</sup>) solution.

For the case with two boundaries, the best gain is 2 * (max over adjacent pairs of min(x, y) minus min over adjacent pairs of max(x, y)), if positive. Intuition: pick two different adjacent pairs, one very high and one very low, and 'cross' them. Take the best of this, of the prefix reversals and of the suffix reversals.
editorial: Write the score as T. Reversing a[l..r] does not change the absolute differences between neighbours inside the range, only the two links at its ends. So the new score is T - |a[l-1]-a[l]| - |a[r]-a[r+1]| + |a[l-1]-a[r]| + |a[l]-a[r+1]|. If the range touches the head only the right link matters (gain |a[0]-a[r+1]| - |a[r]-a[r+1]|), and if it touches the tail only the left link matters. Trying all of these takes O(n) time.

Ranges with two inner boundaries need a trick. The gain equals |a[i]-a[j]| + |a[i+1]-a[j+1]| - |a[i]-a[i+1]| - |a[j]-a[j+1]| for two different links (i, i+1) and (j, j+1). Case analysis on the order of the four values shows the best gain is 2 * (maxLow - minHigh), where maxLow is the largest min(a[i], a[i+1]) and minHigh is the smallest max(a[i], a[i+1]) over all links: the two links come from one 'high' link that lies entirely above the 'low' link, and reversing between them 'crosses' the links so that each gap is replaced with a gap between the two extremes. If the value is not positive, no inner reversal helps.
The answer is T + max(0, prefix gain, suffix gain, inner gain). Everything is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Always compare with a brute force over all ranges when you implement this.
solution:
def maxScoreAfterOneReversal(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    if n < 2:
        return 0
    total = sum(abs(nums[i] - nums[i + 1]) for i in range(n - 1))
    best = 0
    # range touching the head: reverse a[0..r], r < n-1
    for r in range(n - 1):
        best = max(best, abs(nums[0] - nums[r + 1]) - abs(nums[r] - nums[r + 1]))
    # range touching the tail: reverse a[l..n-1], l > 0
    for l in range(1, n):
        best = max(best, abs(nums[l - 1] - nums[n - 1]) - abs(nums[l - 1] - nums[l]))
    # range with two inner boundaries
    max_low = -10 ** 18
    min_high = 10 ** 18
    for i in range(n - 1):
        max_low = max(max_low, min(nums[i], nums[i + 1]))
        min_high = min(min_high, max(nums[i], nums[i + 1]))
    best = max(best, 2 * (max_low - min_high))
    return total + best
